title: AWS S3 US-EAST-1 Service Disruption

severity.usersAffected: Thousands of websites and services worldwide dependent on S3 US-EAST-1
severity.impactUsd: ≈ US$150M+ estimated loss to S&P-500 companies (Cyence, via press)
servicesDown: AWS Service Health Dashboard (couldn't update — hosted on S3)

brief: An authorized S3 engineer running an established capacity-removal playbook mistyped one input; the command removed far more servers than intended, taking down the S3 index and placement subsystems in US-EAST-1. Because a very large number of services (and AWS's own status dashboard) depend on S3, the ~4.5-hour disruption cascaded across a large fraction of the internet.

magnitude.note: Blast radius extreme: S3 is a foundational dependency for a large share of the public internet; cascade reached EC2/EBS/Lambda and even AWS's own status page.

sequenceOfEvents.event: Authorized S3 team member executes an established playbook command to remove a small number of billing-subsystem servers; one input is entered incorrectly, removing a larger server set than intended.

The removed capacity crosses a threshold that forces a FULL restart of two core S3 subsystems: the index subsystem (metadata/location of every US-EAST-1 object, on the read path) and the placement subsystem (allocates storage for new objects, on the write path).
S3 GET/LIST/HEAD/PUT/DELETE/POST APIs return elevated errors region-wide; because the index subsystem serves every request, reads fail even though object data is intact.
Downstream AWS services that depend on S3 in US-EAST-1 degrade: new EC2 instance launches, EBS volumes, and AWS Lambda; thousands of third-party sites/services relying on S3 fail or slow.
The AWS Service Health Dashboard cannot render red status — its own control plane depends on S3 US-EAST-1 — so AWS posts status via the dashboard banner text and @AWSCloud on Twitter.
Placement subsystem recovers; PUT/write path begins to restore for new objects as the index subsystem catches up.
Index subsystem restart + metadata integrity checks complete enough to resume; retrieval operations start returning to normal.
S3 GET/LIST/HEAD (read) operations fully recovered — 4h17m after onset.
S3 PUT/DELETE/POST (write) operations fully recovered — 4h35m after onset; region operating normally.

metrics.label: Root-cause class

rootCause:
Trigger. On 2017-02-28 at 9:37 AM PST, an authorized Amazon S3 team member, working from an established operational playbook, executed a command intended to remove a small number of servers from an S3 subsystem used by the S3 billing process. One of the inputs to that command was entered incorrectly, and as a result a far larger set of servers was removed than intended. This single mistyped input during a routine maintenance action was the proximate ignition of the disruption in the US-EAST-1 (Northern Virginia) Region.

Mechanism. The servers that were inadvertently removed did not belong solely to the billing subsystem; they also supported two other, far more critical S3 subsystems. The first was the index subsystem, which manages the metadata and location information of all S3 objects in the region and is necessary to serve all GET, LIST, PUT, and DELETE requests. The second was the placement subsystem, which manages allocation of new storage during PUT requests and itself requires the index subsystem to be functioning properly to operate correctly. Removing a significant portion of the capacity supporting these subsystems caused each of them to require a full restart, and while they were restarting S3 was unable to service requests. The failure therefore propagated from a peripheral billing-maintenance task into the region-wide object-storage data path.

Why safeguards and redundancy did not prevent a prolonged outage. This was not a data-loss or durability event; it was a capacity-loss and cold-start problem. Because so much capacity was removed at once, the subsystems required a complete restart rather than graceful degradation. Recovery was slow for a structural reason: AWS had not completely restarted the index subsystem or the placement subsystem in its larger regions for many years, and S3 had experienced massive growth over that period, so restarting these services and running the necessary safety checks to validate the integrity of the metadata took longer than expected.

Escalation and blast radius. The outage extended beyond S3. Other US-EAST-1 services that rely on S3 for storage were impaired while the S3 APIs were unavailable, including the S3 console, EC2 new-instance launches, EBS volumes (when data was needed from an S3 snapshot), and AWS Lambda. A compounding communication failure worsened visibility: from the beginning of the event until 11:37 AM PST, AWS could not update individual service status on the Service Health Dashboard because the SHD administration console itself had a dependency on S3 in the affected region. Recovery then proceeded in dependency order: by 12:26 PM PST the index subsystem had activated enough capacity to begin servicing GET, LIST, and DELETE requests; it was fully recovered by 1:18 PM PST; and the placement subsystem, which could only recover once the index subsystem was functional, finished recovery at 1:54 PM PST, at which point S3 was operating normally.
contributingFactors: Insufficient tooling guardrails: the capacity-removal tool accepted an operator input that removed a much larger set of servers than intended and had no safeguard to block removals that would take a subsystem below its minimum required capacity. AWS's committed fix was to modify the tool to remove capacity more slowly and to add safeguards preventing removals below a subsystem's minimum required capacity level.

Hidden/shared infrastructure coupling: servers being removed for the peripheral billing subsystem also underpinned the critical index and placement subsystems, so a low-risk maintenance action had a high-blast-radius effect. The placement subsystem's hard dependency on the index subsystem further serialized and lengthened recovery.

Untested cold-start at scale: the index and placement subsystems had not been completely restarted in the larger regions for many years while S3 grew massively, so the restart plus metadata-integrity safety checks took far longer than expected. AWS reprioritized work to further partition the index subsystem into smaller 'cells' to reduce blast radius and restart time.

Monitoring/communication single point of failure: the Service Health Dashboard administration console depended on S3 in the same failed region, preventing per-service status updates until 11:37 AM PST and obscuring the incident's visibility. AWS's fix was to run the SHD administration console across multiple AWS regions.

Concentration of dependent services in one region: EC2 new-instance launches, EBS snapshot-dependent volumes, Lambda, and the S3 console all relied on US-EAST-1 S3, so a single-region S3 failure cascaded into multiple AWS services.

coe.action: Modify the capacity-removal tool to remove capacity more slowly and to prevent it from taking any subsystem below its minimum required capacity level.
Audit other operational tools for the same class of fast/unsafe capacity actions and add equivalent safety guards.
Partition the S3 index subsystem into smaller cells so recovery is faster and blast radius is smaller; improve restart time of index/placement subsystems.
Change the AWS Service Health Dashboard to run across multiple regions so it can report status even when one region is impaired.

lessonsLearnt: Routine, well-practised operational commands are still high-consequence: guard destructive/scaling actions with rate limits and hard minimum-capacity floors, not just runbooks.
Subsystems that are never restarted accumulate hidden restart risk; exercise cold-start/recovery paths deliberately so real recovery time is known.
Single-region dependency concentration converts a component fault into a systemic one; understand and reduce cross-service blast radius.
Status/observability control planes must not depend on the very system whose health they report.
improvements: Rate-limited capacity operations with enforced minimum-capacity guardrails on the S3 tooling.
Cellularization of the S3 index subsystem to shrink blast radius and speed recovery.
Multi-region AWS Service Health Dashboard so status reporting survives a regional impairment.
Broader operational-tool audit for unsafe fast-acting capacity actions.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism — why a capacity change became an outage
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The command was a routine, authorized capacity-removal action, but the tooling had no floor on how much it could remove and no rate limit. Once removal crossed a threshold, the index and placement subsystems could not continue on the surviving fleet and had to cold-restart. The index subsystem is on the critical path of every S3 request — it resolves the physical location of each object — so its unavailability failed reads even though every byte of object data remained safely stored. The write path failed in parallel because the placement subsystem, which allocates new storage, both went down and itself depends on the index subsystem.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why recovery took ~4.5 hours, not minutes
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: These subsystems had scaled to a very large footprint and had not been fully restarted for years. A cold start therefore had to load and integrity-check an enormous volume of metadata before it could safely serve traffic. The recovery time was dominated not by restarting processes but by the safety/consistency validation those processes must complete first — a latent, untested cost that only surfaced under a full restart. This is the classic 'we never exercise the recovery path, so we don't know its real duration' failure mode.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Blast radius — concentration risk
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: S3 US-EAST-1 is a foundational dependency: many other AWS services (EC2 launch, EBS, Lambda) and a large fraction of the public internet rely on it, often without the dependency being visible to the end operator. A fault in one storage subsystem in one region therefore propagated into a systemic, cross-service event. Critically, AWS's own Service Health Dashboard depended on S3 in the same region, so the primary status channel failed exactly when it was needed — an observability control plane must never share a failure domain with the system it observes.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organizational / systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The proximate cause was human input error, but the incident is better read as a systems-design gap: safe, well-practised operations were allowed to take an irreversible, unbounded action with no guardrail, on subsystems whose recovery characteristics were unknown because they were never exercised. The durable fixes were structural (rate limits, minimum-capacity floors, cellularization, multi-region status) rather than 'be more careful' — the correct engineering response to human-error incidents.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Comparison & pattern
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This sits in the same family as later large cloud events (e.g. the 2020 Kinesis thread-limit event and the 2025 DynamoDB DNS race, both also US-EAST-1 control-plane faults with wide cascades): a single-region control-plane component reaches an untested limit and takes down a shared dependency. The recurring lesson across all of them is blast-radius reduction (cells, regional isolation) and exercising recovery paths, not merely tightening runbooks.

technicalDeepDive:
At an engineering level the failure was a capacity-loss-induced cold restart of stateful metadata subsystems, not a corruption or durability failure. S3 in a region is decomposed into subsystems; the index subsystem is the authoritative store of object metadata and location and sits on the critical path of every GET, LIST, PUT, and DELETE request, while the placement subsystem allocates storage for new objects on PUTs and requires the index subsystem to be functioning properly. The mistyped command input removed a set of servers spanning the billing subsystem plus these two subsystems. Because the removal took capacity below what the running subsystems could tolerate, they could not simply shed the lost nodes and continue; each required a full restart, and during that restart interval S3 was unable to service requests.

The dominant factor in recovery time was the restart of the index subsystem. Restarting it required not just re-provisioning capacity but running safety checks to validate the integrity of the object metadata across the region before it could resume serving traffic. Because S3 had grown massively since the index and placement subsystems had last been fully restarted in the large regions (many years prior), the actual restart-and-validate time far exceeded expectations. The placement subsystem could not begin meaningful recovery until the index subsystem was functional, so the two recoveries were necessarily serialized: the index subsystem reached partial service (GET, LIST, DELETE) at 12:26 PM PST and full recovery at 1:18 PM PST, after which the placement subsystem (PUT path) finished recovery at 1:54 PM PST.

The corrective engineering direction confirms the mechanism. AWS was already partitioning the index subsystem into smaller units it calls 'cells' — which reduces the blast radius and per-unit restart time of any single failure — and reprioritized that work to begin immediately. It also hardened the operational tool to remove capacity more slowly and to refuse removals that would drop any subsystem below its minimum required capacity level, and it changed the Service Health Dashboard administration console to run across multiple AWS regions so status reporting no longer shares fate with the region it reports on.
